content: Self-reference is a phenomenon observed in both natural and formal languages, where a sentence or formula refers to itself either directly, through an intermediate sentence or formula, or via some form of encoding. In philosophy, self-reference also pertains to the capacity of a subject to refer to themselves, as exemplified by the use of the pronoun I in English. This concept becomes possible when there are two logical levels present: a base level and a meta-level. Self-reference is most commonly encountered in disciplines such as mathematics, philosophy, computer programming, and linguistics. However, self-referential statements can sometimes lead to paradoxes, though the significance of these paradoxes may be limited by the concept of antinomy. An example of self-reference in action is the concept of autopoiesis, where a system's logical organization produces the physical structure that, in turn, creates the system itself. In metaphysics, self-reference is associated with subjectivity, while hetero-reference, as described by Niklas Luhmann, corresponds to objectivity. Self-reference also appears in literature when an author refers to their own work within the context of that work. Notable examples include Cervantes' Don Quixote, Denis Diderot's Jacques the Fatalist and His Master, Italo Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveler, various stories by Nikolai Gogol, John Barth's Lost in the Funhouse, and Luigi Pirandello's Six Characters in Search of an Author. This literary device is closely related to the concept of breaking the fourth wall or meta-reference, which often involves self-referential elements. The surrealist painter René Magritte is also well-known for his self-referential works, such as The Treachery of Images, which challenges the viewer's interpretation of the phrase This is not a pipe by questioning whether this refers to the depicted pipe, the painting itself, or the sentence. Self-reference is also employed in tautologies and licensed terminology. For instance, defining a machine as any objects put together mechanically results in a tautology. Such self-references can be intricate, involving entire propositions rather than simple words, and may require acceptance of the terms as self-evident proofs. In computer science, self-reference is exemplified by recursion, where a program unit relies on instances of itself to perform computations. The Lisp programming language is particularly designed to exploit recursion. Object-oriented programming languages use specific keywords to refer to the current instance of an object, such as this in C++, Java, and PHP; self in Smalltalk and Objective-C; and Me in Visual Basic. Examples of Self-Reference Mathematics Tupper's self-referential formula. Sentences This statement is short. I am not the subject of this sentence. 'I' is the subject of this sentence. Which question is also its own answer? 'Yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation' yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation. (This is a version of the liar paradox, an example of indirect self-reference through a quine, leading to a paradox.) The statement that the word 'false' should be interpreted as 'not true' is false. (Another version of the liar paradox.) Russell's paradox: The set of all sets which are not elements of themselves (a set that both includes and does not include itself). The Examples section of this article refers to itself. This sentence exemplifies cacozeila (using rare/foreign words to appear learned). Do not read this. This page intentionally left blank. The Fumblerules Fumblerules are statements of good grammar and writing rules that intentionally violate the very rules they describe. George L. Trigg and William Safire have compiled lists of such rules, but anyone knowledgeable about grammar can create their own. For a comprehensive (though not exhaustive) list, see the List of Fumblerules. Literature Ishmael Reed's poem beware: do not read this poem. The Monster at the End of This Book, which references itself in the title and throughout the story. Abbie Hoffman's Steal This Book. Robert A. Heinlein's The Cat Who Walks Through Walls, which considers the universe (or multiverse) as an author-manipulated object, including the plot of the book itself. Jostein Gaarder's Sophie's World, where the titular character realizes she is a character in a book. Michael Ende's The Neverending Story, which prominently uses self-reference when a character (Atreyu) in a story within the story (also called The Neverending Story) finds a book of the same name, which is the very book the reader is reading.
